corrections.claimed_speedup: Java/OpenJDK (Temurin 27, -Xmx2g, default GC) 0.52 s vs C++/G++ 0.691 s (prod, -O2; the best of the 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ configurations, PGO-instrumented builds excluded), C++/G++/Fast (-O3 -march=native, thin LTO) 0.705 s, C++/G++/Unsafe 0.702 s, best C row C/Gcc/PGO 1.067 s: 1.33x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.36x faster than the -O3 row (derived from page data). Other managed rows in the same file also beat C++: Java/OpenJDK/Serial (-XX:+UseSerialGC -Xmx512m) 0.364 s (1.90x), Kotlin/Scala JVM Opt/Max rows 0.37-0.38 s, C#/AOT 0.501 s; C#/JIT 0.67 s is on par; Julia 2.006 s is slower. corrections.caveats: Margin is modest (1.33x) and most of it arrived with the JDK 27 upgrade; before that Java led by only 1.02-1.13x. Both sides walk the same pre-built AST with the same integer semantics; the only data-structure difference is each language's standard string-keyed hash map for variables (std::unordered_map<std::string,int64_t> in C++, uthash in C, HashMap<String,Long> with boxed Long values in Java). The GC setting matters: the SerialGC row is 1.4x faster than the default-GC row. LangArena's own README calls it a subjective benchmark ('not an objective, peer-reviewed, or industry-standard benchmark suite'), and the author says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages (each port reviewed, checksums verified). The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). Every language runs the same harness: prepare, a warm-up of 20% of the iterations on the same instance, then the timed run (Java calls System.gc() between warm-up and the timed loop), so startup is excluded for all. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -ffast-math, full LTO) and PGO variants are in the same file and still lose on this test. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most of the 50 tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). The 2026-10-05 run is the first on Temurin JDK 27 and on a new Arch Linux host install (the GCC 16 trunk build is unchanged); in the three earlier runs checked (2026-08-14, 2026-09-03, 2026-09-18, OpenJDK 26) Java still led but only narrowly, so most of the margin arrived with the JDK upgrade. Per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results files, not stated by the suite.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Verifier inference from cpp/src/calculator.cpp and CalculatorInterpreter.java: both evaluate the same AST recursively, but every variable read and assignment in C++ goes through std::unordered_map<std::string,int64_t>, which recomputes std::hash of the name string on each find and operator[], and the C port rehashes with uthash plus strlen; java.lang.String caches its hashCode, and the AST (with its name strings) is built once in prepare() and reused, so each name is hashed once for the whole run. HotSpot also inlines the recursive evaluate() and its instanceof chain from the type profile. Allocation and GC of boxed Long values also matter (SerialGC row 0.364 s vs default 0.52 s). Library and runtime effect rather than better codegen for the same machine operations.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=pentium4 Bench.cpp (gcc version 4.0.1, Apple Inc. build 5493, Target: i686-apple-darwin9, so a 32-bit build since no -m64 is passed); javac Bench.java and java -server Bench on Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 1.6.0_07-b06-57, mixed mode)
corrections.caveats: From 2009 with Apple g++ 4.0.1 targeting 32-bit i686 with -march=pentium4 on a Xeon, against a 64-bit HotSpot VM, so the targets differ. No profile-guided optimization or modern speculative devirtualization for C++, which could remove the alternating indirect call; a current GCC or Clang was not measured. One call site microbenchmark (400 million alternating virtual calls incrementing a global), not a general claim. The C++ main() calls bench() 5 times, so the 10 C++ numbers come from two program runs; Java runs 10 iterations in one JVM, so later runs are fully JIT-compiled. C++ times process CPU time (clock()), Java wall time. Benchmark sources are in two other gists (87516 C++, 87518 Java); no license; CPU model not stated beyond '2.8 GHz Xeon'. Mechanism not stated by the author. Tier capped at C.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the author. Verifier inference from gists 87516 and 87518: HotSpot's C2 profiles the x.perform() call site, sees exactly two receiver classes and inlines both bodies behind a type check (bimorphic inlining), turning the loop into straight-line integer adds, while g++ 4.0.1 emits an indirect call through the vtable on every iteration and must reload and store the global counter around it.

notes: Numbers verified on the gist; units are milliseconds per the source gists. Tier C confirmed. Shortcomings to record: 2009 toolchain (g++ 4.0.1, 32-bit pentium4 target vs 64-bit JVM), single-call-site microbenchmark, no CPU model, no license, author's one-off run; same_opt_level stays false because of the 32-bit/pentium4 target mismatch even though C++ was -O3.
